opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how we measure things. When a company announces that their new model is a breakthrough, what they usually mean is that it scored higher on some set of benchmarks. But benchmarks are a pretty narrow window into what a model can actually do. Many of them have been around for years, and the questions or the data have very likely leaked into the training sets of these huge models, which are trained on basically everything that's been scraped from the web. So when a model aces a test, you have to ask: is it reasoning, or has it essentially seen the answers before? Usually we can't tell, because the training data isn't disclosed.

That transparency piece is a big part of my skepticism. With a lot of these flagship models, we don't know what data went in, how big the model is, how much compute was used, or how the evaluation was run. Results are often reported in a blog post or a technical report that wasn't peer reviewed, sometimes with carefully selected comparisons. In any other scientific field, if you said "trust me, it works, but I can't show you how," that wouldn't fly.

There's also the incentive structure. There's an enormous amount of money and attention riding on being seen as the leader, so there's real pressure to frame incremental progress as a leap. And each "breakthrough" usually comes with a much bigger model and much more energy and compute behind it. My work focuses a lot on that environmental cost. If we're getting a few percentage points on a leaderboard in exchange for orders of magnitude more energy, I think we should be honest about that trade-off instead of just celebrating the number.

And finally, a benchmark score doesn't tell you how a model behaves in the real world, for the people who'll actually use it or be affected by it. Does it work in other languages? Is it biased? Does it fail in weird ways? Those questions matter far more to me than whether it beat the last model by a point on a multiple-choice test. So I'm not saying progress isn't happening. I just want us to be much more rigorous and much more humble about how we talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark questions may have leaked into training data and that undisclosed training data makes it hard to tell whether a model reasoned or had seen answers before.

r002.rationale: It discusses models scoring higher on benchmarks and notes many benchmarks have existed for years, but does not say state-of-the-art claims often introduce a new dataset or evaluation task.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think a lot of it comes from spending years actually trying to evaluate these models rigorously, and seeing how much of the gap there is between what gets announced and what you can actually verify. When a company puts out a press release saying their new model has achieved some breakthrough, usually what's behind that is a number on a benchmark. And benchmarks are really fragile things. Many of them are saturated, many of them have leaked into training data, and most of them were designed to measure something fairly narrow that then gets extrapolated into these grand claims about reasoning or understanding or general intelligence.

The other piece is that we often can't reproduce any of it. The models are closed, the training data is undisclosed, sometimes even the evaluation setup isn't fully described. So you're essentially being asked to take a company's word for it, and that company has a very strong commercial incentive to frame things as a breakthrough. That's not how science is supposed to work. In any other field, if someone said "we made a huge discovery but we can't show you the data or the method," you'd be rightly skeptical.

And then there's the question of what "capability" even means. A model scoring well on a math test doesn't mean it can do math the way a person does. We've seen so many cases where you perturb the question slightly, change the numbers or the phrasing, and performance falls apart. So I'm not saying progress isn't happening. It clearly is. But I think the honest framing is "this model does better on this specific task under these specific conditions," and that's a lot less exciting than "breakthrough," which is exactly why we don't hear it that way.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark scores and their limitations, but does not say that state-of-the-art claims often introduce a new dataset or evaluation task.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by a breakthrough. Often, we see a model doing well on a benchmark, and that gets translated into a much broader claim about what it understands or can do. But a benchmark measures performance on a particular set of tasks. It doesn’t necessarily tell us how reliably that capability transfers to a different setting.

There’s also the question of what went into training the model. If we don’t know what data it saw, it’s hard to disentangle generalization from exposure to similar examples. So I want to see independent testing, transparent methods, and an examination of where the model fails—not just a compelling demo.

That doesn’t mean there isn’t progress. It means the scope of the claim should match the evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we’re calling a breakthrough. A model doing better on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean it has acquired some fundamentally new capability. It might mean that we’ve improved the way we train it, or that the benchmark isn’t really measuring what we think it is.

What I want to see is evidence that goes beyond a few impressive examples. Does the capability hold up across different situations? Can other researchers reproduce the result? What are the limitations? When we don’t have access to the training data or enough detail about the evaluation, it’s hard to answer those questions. So my skepticism is really about the gap between what’s demonstrated and what’s claimed.

r001.rationale: The response says limited access to training data makes claims harder to assess, but does not say capabilities may have been learned from training examples rather than emerging.
